On this hillside, two distinct voices resonate with me. One is the voice of the day, the other of the night. Throughout the day the robin sings his song with unflagging spirit. It is not a very brilliant song, but it is indomitably cheerful. Regardless of the weather—be it rainy or sunny, chilly or warm—his song fills the November air from dawn until dusk. This little creature, adorned in his bright red vest, flits from tree to tree, often landing on the fence before hopping to the garden path, and finally to the door that leads into the kitchen. If you will give him decent encouragement he will come on to your hand and take his meal with absolute confidence in your good faith. Then he will trip away and resume his song on the fence.

Some critics have harsh words for the robin, labeling him selfish and claiming he can be difficult to live with. Yet, in my eyes, he stands as one of nature's most steadfast and uplifting companions. He is a bringer of good tidings—a philosopher who insists that we are masters of our fate and that winter is just the time when there is some sense in being an optimist. He seems to convey that anyone can adopt a hopeful outlook when days are long, the air is warm, and food is abundant; however, it is in those bleak moments when others begin to grumble that he dons his brightest waistcoat, tunes his best whistle, and comes forth to remind us that the indomitable spirit surpasses any circumstance.

As night falls and the valley below is shrouded in darkness, another voice emerges—the sorrowful lament of the owl from the thicket beyond the orchard. The day is over, he says, and all is lost. "Tu-whit, tu-whoo." He insists that he alone remains to recount the conclusion of all matters. "Tu-whit, tu-whoo." I've told it all before a thousand times, but you wouldn't believe me. "Tu-whit, tu-whoo." The darkness envelops us, the cold wind bites, and the earth feels like a grave. "Tu-whit, tu-whoo." Where are the songs of spring and the leaves of summer? "Tu-whit, tu-whoo." Where the red-cheeked apple that hung on the bough and the butterfly that fluttered in the sunshine? All, all are gone. "Tu-whit, tu-whoo … Tu-whit, tu-whoo … Tu-whit, tu-whoo…."

A cheerless fellow. Some people find him an intolerable companion. I was talking at dinner in London a few nights ago to a woman who has a house in Sussex, and I found that she had not been there for some time.

"I used to find the owl endurable," said she, "but since the war I have found him unbearable. He hoots all night and makes me so depressed that I feel that I shall go mad."

"And so you come and listen to the owl in London?" I said.

"The owl in London?" she replied, puzzled.

"Yes," I said, "the owl that hoots in Carmelite Street and Printing House Square."

"Oh," she said, "but that owl is utterly ridiculous. The country owl, on the other hand, carries such a grave demeanor."

"He says a very foolish thing In such a solemn way,"

I murmured.

"Yes, but in the silence and the darkness there doesn't seem any answer to him."

"Madame," I said, "if you will look up at the stars you will find a very complete answer."

I confess that I find the owl not only tolerable but stimulating. I like to hear the pessimist really let himself go. It is the vague, undefined fears that can immobilize us, yet when this owl articulates the situation in its most dismal light, I begin to feel a sense of defiance and determination. If this is the worst he can conjure, then let us strive to uncover the best and work towards achieving it. "This task is impossible," the pessimist might tell Cobden. "Indeed," said that great man. "Then the sooner we set about doing it the better." Oh, dear owl, are you claiming all is lost? You wait till the dawn comes, and hear what that little chap in the red waistcoat has to say about it. He's got quite another tale to tell, and it's a much more likely tale than yours. I shall go to bed and leave you to Gummidge in the trees until the sun comes up and tells you what a dismal fraud you are.

"Tu-whit, tu-whoo," the owl responds to me.

Indeed, dear sir, but you have uttered that lament every night I have known you, and yet the sun consistently rises, bringing spring once more, along with blooming flowers and fields bursting with harvest.

"Tu-whit, tu-whoo."

Oh, bother you. You could easily serve as a sensational headline in the Daily Mail.

No doubt the owl is quite happy in his way. Louis XV once articulated the owl’s philosophy when he remarked, "Let us entertain ourselves by making ourselves miserable." I suspect the poor creature finds some twisted joy in his own despair. I have always thought that, secretly, Mrs. Gummidge had a roaring time. She really enjoyed being miserable and making everybody about her miserable. I have known such people, and I daresay you have known them, too—people who nurse unhappiness with the passion of a miser. They are having the time of their lives now. They go about saying, "Tu-whit, tu-whoo! The Russians are beaten again, or if they are not beaten they will be. Tu-whit, tu-whoo! We're slackers and laggards, and the Germans are overwhelming us. Tu-whit, tu-whoo. They're on the way to India and Egypt, and nothing will stop them. All hope is lost." But I notice that they enjoy a beef-steak as much as anybody, and do not refuse their soup though they salt it with their tears.

I find the anecdote about Stonewall Jackson and the owl particularly telling. The owl was a general, and he rushed up to Jackson in the crisis of the first battle of Bull's Run, crying "All is lost! We're beaten!" "Oh," said Jackson, "if that's so I'd advise you to keep it to yourself." A half-hour later, Jackson's brigade made a charge that turned the tide of the battle. I can only wonder what became of the owl, but I suspect he continued to lament, "Tu-whit-ing" and "Tu-whoo-ing" until the very end. The owl can't help being an owl.

Ah, there is little red waistcoat singing on the fence. Let’s find him a worm, shall we?

The conclusion that we had to relinquish the governess-cart signified that a new home for Polly needed to be secured.

Polly is a roan pony, notably plump, and particularly so in recent weeks due to the limited diet of meadow grass. She had been with us (this is my neighbour's story, as told to me during the War: a very charming neighbour who keeps her temper at croquet)—Polly had been with us so long as to become, as ponies peculiarly can, a member of the family, so that to part with her savoured of treachery. Necessity, however, knows no law and sanctifies no memory, and the distasteful preparations were therefore begun. The first was the framing of the advertisement; which is not the simple matter that it might appear to be, because so much depends upon the choice of adjective: the selected word must both allure and (in our case) keep within the bounds of truth. What are the qualities most valued in a pony, we had to ask ourselves. Celerity? Polly was fixed in her determination not to exceed the speed limit, at any rate on outward journeys. Willingness? Polly could be desperately stubborn. Strength? Yes, she was robust. Youth? Well, she had joined our family a decade ago and was no longer a young foal. After much serious contemplation, which could be likened to the deliberations at Versailles, we settled on describing Polly as either a "strong useful pony" or a "useful strong pony." Eventually, we agreed on the phrasing "Pony, strong, useful" and sent the advertisement off to the local paper, often humorously referred to as the county chronicle.

The next pressing matter was determining an appropriate price. Here expert opinion was resorted to, in the shape of Mr. Edmead, the butcher. No one knows more about ponies than butchers do, and Mr. Edmead is exceptionally wise.

"Taking everything into consideration," he said, "I think that twenty-five pounds would be a fair price."

We clung to each other for support. Twenty-five pounds! And we had given only nine pounds all those years ago. Why had we not taken up pony breeding as a hobby? Mr. Edmead elaborated that the War had inflated the value of ponies. Yes, taking everything into consideration, twenty-five pounds was a fair price. We ought to get that. In fact, if he had been in need of a pony he would have given that himself; but just then he was well supplied, and Polly was, he feared, not quite fast enough for him. Good morning.

Those seeking to buy a pony share a striking similarity. They are clean-shaven and wear hard round hats, and the collars of their overcoats are carelessly treated so that they are half up and half down. They carry sticks. Also, although they want a pony, they don't want one at quite such a figure. Each man who came to inspect Polly echoed a similar sentiment: while they recognized her as a strong useful pony, she ultimately did not meet their needs. Day after day Polly was examined. They opened her mouth and shook their heads, they felt her knees and her hocks, they looked at her with narrow eyes from near by and from far, they rattled their sticks in their hard hats, they gave her sudden cuts and prods. As time wore on, desperation began to set in.

While we were fond of Polly, the urgency of selling her grew stronger. Things should be done quickly. Then, a market gardener named Fox, a jovial and portly man, arrived. And Polly was again led forth and again subjected to every test known to pony-buyers. All was going well, and would have gone well, but for Vivian.

Who, you ask, is Vivian? We should be better prepared for the irruption of new characters. True, but this is not my story, but my nice neighbour's.

Vivian is a small boy who had known Polly all his life, and who by some mischance wandered out from his lessons in the morning-room at the precise moment when Mr. Fox, who obviously was attracted by Polly, was making up his mind to pay the full money. I should clarify that Vivian possesses a charm that leads him to view the world as a playground designed for making friends, drawing him to laborers who work outdoors. The moment he spotted Mr. Fox's kind face, he eagerly added him to his list of acquaintances.

"Run away, Vivian," I said. "It's not play-time yet, and we're busy."

"Are you going to buy Polly?" Vivian asked Mr. Fox by way of a suitable rejoinder to my command.

"I was considering it," Mr. Fox replied, turning to me. "How old do you estimate she is? She looks to me about twelve."

The figure was so low that I nodded assent, but Vivian spoilt it by exclaiming, "Oh, mother, and Mr. Brooks says she's seventeen if she's a day, and I'm sure she's a day."

Mr. Fox became thoughtful. "Mr. Brooks said that, did he?" he inquired.

I felt that I couldn't tell Vivian again to go in, because it would look as though I feared his frankness; which, to be candid, I did. All I could do was to hope for the best.

"She’s quite docile; accustomed to traffic and so forth?" Mr. Fox asked.

Vivian then began to chuckle. This nostalgic laughter, reflecting on past events—he often revisits old stories, and his giggles are quite endearing; however, in this moment, I felt a knot tighten in my stomach.

"Don't you remember, mother," he began, "that day when she was frightened by the traction engine and ran into the grocer's shop?"

Mr. Fox, whose large hand now held my son's tiny one, adopted a serious expression.

"That's against her in my business," he said.

I quickly interjected, "Oh, that was ages ago! She’s quite steady now. Don't you remember, Vivian, it was on your fifth birthday?"

"No," said Vivian, "that was on my seventh birthday—something funny always happens on my birthdays," he explained to Mr. Fox—"it was on my fifth birthday that Polly fell down."

"She's been down, has she?" said Mr. Fox ominously.

The ensuing exchanges grew increasingly disheartening. I had no intention of concealing anything; Mr. Edmead knew the pony's whole history when he valued her; but Vivian's presence made me nervous, painfully self-conscious; I felt my face burning and knew that I must suggest duplicity.

Mr. Fox, to his credit, navigated the situation skillfully. He asked Vivian no questions; indeed he talked of other things than defective ponies; but I could see his mind working; I could see pound after pound dropping away from the grand total.

Well, that's the story. Mr. Fox led Polly away some ten minutes later, leaving in her stead a cheque. But it was not for twenty-five pounds—Vivian saw to that.

The moral? The moral is: when your husband is in Mesopotamia and the time comes to sell the pony, lock your cherubic son in the nursery.

People accuse journalism of being too personal; but to me it has always seemed far too impersonal. While journalism is meant to strip away the layers of private lives, it often seems to create translucent but blinding barriers between individuals. The Yellow Press is abused for exposing facts which are private; I wish the Yellow Press did anything so valuable. A clear illustration of this is the disorienting experience of meeting someone in real life after having encountered them countless times in newspapers; the disconnect can be striking. The Yellow Pressman seems to have no power of catching the first fresh fact about a man that dominates all after impressions. For instance, before I met Bernard Shaw I heard that he spoke with a reckless desire for paradox or a sneering hatred of sentiment; but I never knew till he opened his mouth that he spoke with an Irish accent, which is more important than all the other criticisms put together.

Journalism lacks a sufficient personal touch. So far from digging out private personalities, it cannot even report the obvious personalities on the surface. Now there is one vivid and even bodily impression of this kind which we have all felt when we met great poets or politicians, but which never finds its way into the newspapers. I mean the impression that they are much older than we thought they were. We tend to associate greatness with past achievements, which typically occurred years ago; thus, many who idolized the youthful Napoleon of Marengo must have been surprised to encounter the more corpulent Napoleon of Leipzig.

I recall reading a newspaper piece detailing how an emerging politician addressed the House of Lords with a youthful exuberance. It described his “brave young voice” echoing throughout the chamber. I also remember that I met him some days after, and he was considerably older than my own father. I mention this truth for only one purpose: all this generalisation leads up to only one fact—the fact that I once met a great man who was younger than I expected.

.....

I had come over the wooded wall from the villages about Epsom, and down a stumbling path between trees towards the valley in which Dorking lies. A warm sunlight was working its way through the leafage; a sunlight which though of saintless gold had taken on the quality of evening. It was such sunlight as reminds a man that the sun begins to set an instant after noon. It seemed to lessen as the wood strengthened and the road sank.

I had a sensation peculiar to such entangled descents; I felt that the treetops that closed above me were the fixed and real things, certain as the level of the sea; but that the solid earth was every instant failing under my feet. Soon, the brilliant sunlight transformed into mere splashes of light, resembling fiery stars scattered in a canopy of green. Around me in that emerald twilight were trunks of trees of every plain or twisted type; it was like a chapel supported on columns of every earthly and unearthly style of architecture.

Without intention my mind grew full of fancies on the nature of the forest; on the whole philosophy of mystery and force. For the meaning of woods is the combination of energy with complexity. They are not at all crude or primitive; rather, they are characterized by a rich delicacy. Unique shapes that an artist would copy or a philosopher watch for years if he found them in an open plain are here mingled and confounded; but it is not a darkness of deformity. It is a darkness of life; a darkness of perfection. And I began to think how much of the highest human obscurity is like this, and how much men have misunderstood it. People often assert that theology became convoluted due to its lifelessness. Believe me, if it had been dead it would never have become elaborate; it is only the live tree that grows too many branches.

.....

As I walked, the trees gradually receded from one another, and I emerged into a field of tall grass alongside a road. I was caught off guard by how late the day had advanced; it felt as though this valley had its own unique sunset. Continuing along the road as directed, I passed through a modest gate that marked the transition from the woods to a garden. It was as if the curious courtesy and fineness of that character I was to meet went out from him upon the valley; for I felt on all these things the finger of that quality which the old English called “faërie”; it is the quality which those can never understand who think of the past as merely brutal; it is an ancient elegance such as there is in trees. I went through the garden and saw an old man sitting by a table, looking smallish in his big chair. He was already an invalid, and his hair and beard were both white; not like snow, for snow is cold and heavy, but like something feathery, or even fierce; rather they were white like the white thistledown. I approached him closely; he extended his frail hand and, in that moment, I was struck by the surprising youthfulness in his eyes. He was the one great man of the old world whom I have met who was not a mere statue over his own grave.

Although he was deaf, he spoke with a torrent of words. He did not talk about the books he had written; he was far too much alive for that. He talked about the books he had not written. He unrolled a purple bundle of romances which he had never had time to sell. He casually asked me to pen one of these narratives for him, as if he were requesting a favor from a neighbor. It was a splendid and frantic story, a sort of astronomical farce. It was all about a man who was rushing up to the Royal Society with the only possible way of avoiding an earth-destroying comet; and it showed how, even on this huge errand, the man was tripped up at every other minute by his own weakness and vanities; how he lost a train by trifling or was put in gaol for brawling. That is only one of them; there were ten or twenty more. Another, I dimly remember, was a version of the fall of Parnell; the idea that a quite honest man might be secret from a pure love of secrecy, of solitary self-control. As I left that garden, I was enveloped in a blurred sense of the infinite possibilities inherent in creative literature. This feeling intensified as I reentered the woods, for a forest is akin to a grand palace with countless intersecting corridors. I really had the feeling that I had seen the creative quality; which is supernatural. I had seen what Virgil calls the Old Man of the Forest: I had seen an elf. The trees loomed behind me as I departed, and I have never seen him since; now I know I will not see him again, for he passed away last Tuesday.

"Look at Peggy with that dreadful cat again—the one-eyed creature from next door," someone exclaimed. I turned my gaze outside and indeed saw Peggy coming down the garden path, cradling in her arms the one-eyed feline from over the fence. Peggy likes the animal in spite of its one eye. I am not sure that she does not like it all the more because of its one eye. I think she has an idea that if she nurses the cat it forgets that it has only one eye and recovers its happiness. She has a passion for all four-legged creatures. I've witnessed her spend an entire day gathering handfuls of grass from the orchard, eagerly delivering them to the donkey or horse in the neighboring paddock. When there are no animals to engage with, she improvises by donning horseshoes on her hands and feet, mimicking the sound of a horse trotting about. Though her compassion embraces all four-legged beings, her deepest affections appear to be reserved for those who are disabled or disadvantaged.

It is only among children that we find the quality of charity sufficiently strong to forgive deformity. The instinct to turn away from physical flaws is deeply ingrained; it seems to be an evolutionary trait aimed at preserving the ideal forms of life. We call these forms beauty and the departure from them ugliness, and it is from "beauty's rose," as Shakespeare says, that "we desire increase." If you shudder at the touch of a withered hand or at the sight of a one-eyed cat, it is because you feel that they are a menace to the established forms of life. You are unconsciously playing the part of policeman for nature. You are the guardian of its traditions when you blush at the glance of two eyes and shudder at the glance of one.

And yet it is not impossible to fall in love with the physically defective and sincerely to believe that they are beautiful. Take that incident mentioned by Descartes. He said that when he was a child he used to play with a little girl who had a squint, and that to the end of his days he liked people who squinted. In this instance, the memories associated with that squinted gaze infused a sense of charm into what might initially seem a deformity. The squint brought back to him the memory of the Golden Age, and through the mist of that memory it was transmuted into loveliness.

Nor is it memory alone that will work the miracle. Intellectual sympathy will do it, too. Wilkes was renowned for his ugliness, but he claimed that, given half an hour's start, he would win the smiles of any woman against any competitor. When one of his female supporters defended him against a remark regarding his squint, she declared, "Of course he does; but he doesn't squint more than a man of his genius ought to squint." It wasn’t only women who were captivated by Wilkes. Who can forget the scene when Tom Davies brought him into the company of Dr. Johnson, who hated Wilkes' Radicalism, and would never willingly have consented to meet him? Initially, Johnson remained aloof, but eventually, he succumbed to the allure of Wilkes' conversation.

Similarly, Johnson regarded his wife as the epitome of beauty, despite the fact that most others saw her as plain and unremarkable. To the rest of the world she was extraordinarily plain and commonplace, but to Johnson she was the mirror of beauty. "Pretty creature," he would say with a sigh in referring to her after her death.

And there, I fancy, we touch the root of the matter. The sense of beauty is in one respect an affair of the soul, and only superficially an aesthetic quality. We begin with a common bias in favor of certain forms—those that nature has instilled in us as ideals. They are the forms with which nature has made us familiar, and we seek to perpetuate them. But if the conventionally beautiful form is allied with spiritual ugliness it ceases to be beautiful to us, and if the conventionally ugly form is allied with spiritual beauty that beauty irradiates the physical deficiency. The soul dominates the senses. Francis Thompson expresses the idea very beautifully when he says:—

I cannot tell what beauty is her dole, Who cannot see her features for her soul. As birds see not the casement for the sky.

But there is another sense in which beauty is the most matter-of-fact thing. I can conceive that if the human family had developed only one eye, and that planted in the centre of the forehead, the appearance of a person with two eyes would be as offensive to our sense of beauty as a hand that consisted not of fingers but of thumbs. We would likely view the two-eyed individual with a blend of curiosity and disdain, much like how we currently find ourselves observing the bearded woman in a sideshow. We should not go to admire his two eyes, any more than we go to admire the beard; we should go to enjoy a pleasant sense of disgust at his misfortune and a comfortable satisfaction at the fact that we had not been the victims of such a calamity. We should roll our single eye with a proud feeling that we were in the true line of beauty, from which the two-eyed man in front was a hideous and fantastic departure.

In essence, beauty serves as a tribute to necessity. In equipping itself for the struggle for existence humanity has found that it is convenient to have two eyes and a stereoscopic vision, just as it is convenient to have four fingers on the hand and one thumb instead of five thumbs. Our physical attributes have been shaped by the demands of survival. And the more perfectly they fulfil that supreme condition the more beautiful we declare them to be. Our conceptions of beauty, therefore, are not fixed; they are contingent upon our biological needs. They are the humble servants of our necessity. Two eyes are essential for navigating our world, and thus, we come to cherish them. The more adept they are at their functions, the more we are drawn to them, declaring them beautiful.

I think that Peggy, nursing her one-eyed cat there in the sun, has not yet accepted our creed of beauty. She will be as conventional as the rest of us when her frocks are longer.

On those rare occasions when I put on my best clothes and venture into society, I am always astonished at the number of people in it whom I do not know. I have stood in a crowded ball-room, or sat in a crowded restaurant, and reflected that, of all the hundreds of souls present, there was not one of whose existence I had previously had any suspicion. Yet, each one of them leads a life of tremendous significance—not just to themselves, but also to a multitude of friends and family. Each day, they face their own challenges, and there inevitably comes a moment for each individual when the rest of the world, including—much to my chagrin—myself, seems utterly irrelevant. That I had lived all these years in contented ignorance of their existence makes me a little ashamed.

Today, dressed in my oldest attire, I have perused the index of The Times Literary Supplement, and I find myself grappling with a profound sense of shame over my lack of knowledge regarding numerous books. Of novels alone there seem to be about 900. To write even a thoroughly futile novel is, to my thinking, a work of extraordinary endurance; yet in, say, 600 houses this work has been going on, and I (and you, and all of us) have remained utterly unmoved. Well, I have been making up for my indifference this morning. I have been reading the titles of the books. That is not so good (or bad) as reading the books themselves, but it enables me to say that I have heard of such and such a novel, and in some cases it does give me a slight clue to what goes on inside.

In my estimation, the most enjoyable aspect of crafting a novel must be the selection of a title. My idea of a title is that it should be something which reflects the spirit of your work and gives the hesitating purchaser some indication of what he is asked to buy. To call your book Ethnan Frame or Esther Grant or John Temple or John Merridew (I quote from the index) is to help the reader not at all. All it tells him is that one of the characters inside will be called John or Esther—a matter, probably, of indifference to him. Conversely, a title like Phyllis does hint at the nature of the narrative. No novel with a tragic ending, no powerful realistic novel, would be called Phyllis. I would surmise that this novel is a delightful exploration of suburban life, predominantly conveyed through dialogue, featuring Phyllis as an endearing character, albeit somewhat unkind regarding that initial box of chocolates he sent her. However, she married him in the end all right.

But if you don't call your book Phyllis or John Temple or Mrs. Elmsley, what—I hear you asking—are you to call it? You might consider the title Kapak, as I have noticed someone has done. The beauty of Kapak as a title is that if you come into the shop by the back entrance, and so approach the book from the wrong end, it is still Kapak. A title that reads the same in either direction provides substantial advantage to the author. Besides, in this particular case there is a mystery about Kapak which one is burning to solve. Is it the bride's pet name for her father-in-law, the password into the magic castle, or that new stuff with which you polish brown boots? Or is it only a camera? Let us buy the book at once and find out.

Another mystery title is The Man with Thicker Beard, which probably means something. It is like Kapak in this, that it reads equally well backwards; but it is not so subtle. Still, it would likely entice readers to explore its contents. On the other hand, A Welsh Nightingale and a Would-be Suffragette is just the sort of book to which we would not be tempted by the title. The mere act of asking a shopkeeper, "Do you have A Welsh Nightingale and a Would-be Suffragette?" feels cumbersome. If we were to forget the title and instead inquire about a would-be nightingale and a Welsh suffragette, or perhaps a wood nightingale and a Welsh rabbit, or even the Welsh suffragette's night in jail, we would rapidly regret not opting for something straightforward like Greed, Earth, or Jonah.

And this is why a French title is always such a mistake. Authors must bear in mind that their readers not only need to order the book verbally but also recommend it to their acquaintances. So I think Mr. Oliver Onions made a mistake when he called his collection of short stories Pot au Feu. It is a good title, but it is the sort of title to which the person to whom you are recommending the book always answers, "What?" When faced with such confusion after attempting to pronounce the title in your best Parisian accent, the only recourse is to shift the topic entirely. But it is quite time that we came to some sort of decision as to what makes the perfect title. Kapak, as mentioned, may attract buyers, though some might find it somewhat unfair. While it excels commercially, it does not fulfill our initial criteria; the title must resonate with the book's essence. In one sense Five Gallons of Gasolene does this, but of course nobody could ask for that in a book-shop.

Well, then, here is a perfect title, Their High Adventure. That explains itself just sufficiently. When a Man's Married, For Henri and Navarre, and The King Over the Water are slightly more overt, yet still effective. The Love Story of a Mormon makes no attempt to deceive the purchaser, but it can hardly be called a beautiful title. Melody in Silver, on the other hand, is beautiful, but for this reason makes one afraid to buy it, lest there should be disappointment within. As I scan the index, I find myself relieved by the multitude of novels I have yet to read. In most of them there would be disappointment. And really one only reads books nowadays so as to be able to say to one's neighbour on one's rare appearances in society, "HAVE you read The Forged Coupon, and WHAT do you think of The Muck Rake?" And for this an index is quite enough.

The future is uncertain, and while we cannot predict how we will react in dire situations, we are often acutely aware of our limitations. We may not know, for example, what kind of figure we should cut in a burning house, and even less in a burning ship: to what extent the suddenness and dreadfulness of the danger would paralyse our best impulses, or even so bring out our worst as to make us wild beasts for self-protection. Although true emotional crises are infrequent, and no amount of preparation can truly equip us for them, we can only hope that we would act appropriately in those moments. But most of us know with certainty what our limitations are. I, for instance, know that I cannot recite in public and that no circumstances could make me. Facing a crowd, even one made up of friends, fills me with a dread that surpasses any physical danger I might encounter. And by recite I do not mean the placid repetition of an epigram, but the downright translation of dramatic verse into gesture and grimace. The bare idea of such a performance fills me with creeping terror.

The spectacle of any real reciter, however self-possessed and decent, at his work, suffuses me with shame. I myself have in my brief experience of them blushed more for reciters than the whole army of them could ever have blushed for themselves. Even the great humane Brandram when he adopted the falsetto which he deemed appropriate to Shakespeare's women sent the hot tide of misery to my face, while over his squeaking in "Boots at the Holly Tree Inn" I had to close my eyes. Brandram, however, was not strictly a reciter in the way that I mean: rather was he an actor who chose to do a whole play by himself without costumes or scenery. The reciters I refer to typically focus on individual pieces and often consist of enthusiastic amateurs who remain undeterred by the scathing critiques in Mr. Anstey's "Burglar Bill," entertaining at various gatherings or smoking concerts. Their leading poet when I was younger was the versatile Dagonet, who had a humble but terribly effective derivative in the late Mr. Eaton, the author of "The Fireman's Wedding," and their leading humourist was the writer of a book called "T Leaves." Their era also introduced "Kissing Cup's Race," a piece that Mr. Lewis Sydney and "Q" worked tirelessly to render obsolete. Today, I find myself at a loss regarding the current favorites in recitation, as I have not encountered any in quite some time.

But from those old days when escape was more difficult comes the memory of the worst and the best that I ever heard. The worst was "Papa's Letter," a popular poem of sickly and irresistible sentimentality, which used to call out the handkerchiefs in battalions. The nominal narrator is a young widow whose golden-haired boy wishes to join her in writing a letter to his father. This was at a time before Sir Oliver Lodge had established wireless telephony between heaven and earth. Since the child cannot write she turns him into a letter himself by fancifully sticking a stamp on his forehead. He then dashes outside to play but is tragically struck by a runaway horse, and—

Who wrote this saccharine tragedy I cannot say, but I once found the name of W. S. Gilbert against it on a programme. Could he possibly have been the author? The psychology of humour is so curious....

So much for the worst recitations. The best that I can recall I heard twenty-five years ago, and have only just succeeded in tracking to print. It was recited at a Bohemian gathering of which I made one in a Fleet Street tavern, the reciter being a huge Scottish painter with a Falstaffian head. His jovial, ruddy face and exuberantly white hair and beard made quite an impression. I had never crossed paths with him before or after that evening, yet the memory of his presence amidst the swirling tobacco smoke remains vivid. When called upon to share something, the towering figure claimed he would recite James Boswell's authentic opinion of Dr. Johnson. A thrill of expectation ran through the room, for it appeared that the artist was famous for this effort. For someone like me, unfamiliar with the work, the title alone was enticing enough. With a depth of humor that seemed to require crossing borders, he presented the piece while perched tipsily on the edge of an imaginary bed. Every word told, and at the end the greatness of the Great Cham was a myth. For years I tried to find this poem; but no one could tell me anything about it. Here and there was a man who had heard it, but as to authorship he knew nothing. The Scotsman was no more, I discovered. It was only last year that I learned the name of the author: Godfrey Turner, a prominent figure in Fleet Street during the 'sixties and 'seventies. A chance meeting with his son led me to various humorous anthologies, one of which, H. S. Leigh's "Jeux d'Esprit," contained the poem. Like many of the best recitations, it does not read famously in cold blood, but as delivered by my Scottish painter it carried big guns. Here it is; but there seems to be an error in the beginning of the third stanza, unless Bozzy's muzziness is being indicated:—

While the piece was splendid in the hands of that Scottish artist, I find no desire to hear it again. Nor, indeed, do I want to hear any recitation again, unless it is given in mimicry of some one else. Under those conditions I could listen to anything, so powerful is the attraction of the mimic's art. Possibly part of this fascination may be due to one's own inability to imitate too; be that as it may, no mimic who is at all capable ever bores me, and all fill me with wonder. Of course I am conscious that many of the imitators who throng the stage are nothing but pickpockets: too lazy and too mean to acquire novelties of their own, they annex snatches of the best songs of the moment under the plea of burlesquing the original singers. But even so, I often find myself immorally glad that they figure in the programme.

What stands out about talented mimics is their ability to not only replicate vocal tones but also to capture the essence of a person's conversational style. I recall an instance where a particularly skilled performer gave a spontaneous impression of a renowned scholar he had just met. Interestingly, during that impersonation, the mimic, despite being somewhat uneducated, seemed to adopt vocabulary and phrasing that I am certain he did not possess in his everyday speech. It was almost as if, for a brief interval, the mimic was the scholar, though always with the drop of ridicule or mischief added. It would be interesting to know if, when anyone is being impersonated as intensely as this, any virtue departs from him—whether he is, for the moment, by so much the less himself.

In the town of Belfort, I find a seat on the street and observe my surroundings. We talk in a cant phrase of the Man in the Street, but the Frenchman is the man in the street. Things quite central for him are connected with these lamp-posts and pavements; everything from his meals to his martyrdoms. When first an Englishman looks at a French town or village his first feeling is simply that it is uglier than an English town or village; when he looks again he sees that this comparative absence of the picturesque is chiefly expressed in the plain, precipitous frontage of the houses standing up hard and flat out of the street like the cardboard houses in a pantomime—a hard angularity allied perhaps to the harshness of French logic. Upon a third glance, it becomes apparent that this is primarily because French homes do not feature front gardens. The vague English spirit loves to have the entrance to its house softened by bushes and broken by steps. It likes to have a little anteroom of hedges half in the house and half out of it; a green room in a double sense. The Frenchman desires no such little pathetic ramparts or halting places, for the street itself is a thing natural and familiar to him.

.....

While the French may lack front gardens, their streets serve as a collective front garden for everyone. These thoroughfares are adorned with trees and occasionally fountains. The street is the Frenchman’s tavern, for he drinks in the street. It is his dining-room, for he dines in the street. It is his British Museum, for the statues and monuments in French streets are not, as with us, of the worst, but of the best, art of the country, and they are often actually as historical as the Pyramids. The street again is the Frenchman’s Parliament, for France has never taken its Chamber of Deputies so seriously as we take our House of Commons, and the quibbles of mere elected nonentities in an official room seem feeble to a people whose fathers have heard the voice of Desmoulins like a trumpet under open heaven, or Victor Hugo shouting from his carriage amid the wreck of the second Republic. The street, therefore, is not merely a place for dining and drinking; it is also a battleground where the Frenchman fights and sometimes perishes, imbibing the streets with a significance that transcends the ordinary.

Consider, for instance, the unassuming lamp-post. In London a lamp-post is a comic thing. We think of the intoxicated gentleman embracing it, and recalling ancient friendship. But in Paris a lamp-post is a tragic thing. For we think of tyrants hanged on it, and of an end of the world. There was a satirical Republican newspaper in Paris called LA LANTERNE, and one might find amusement at the thought of a British publication titled THE LAMP POST. We have said, then, that the Frenchman is the man in the street; that he can dine in the street, and die in the street. And if I ever pass through Paris and find him going to bed in the street, I shall say that he is still true to the genius of his civilisation. All that is good and all that is evil in France is alike connected with this open-air element. French democracy and French indecency are alike part of the desire to have everything out of doors. Compared to a café, a public-house is a private house.

Two particular reasons prompted these reflections while I wandered the streets of Belfort.

First of all, it lies close upon the boundary of France and Germany, and boundaries are the most beautiful things in the world. To love anything is to love its boundaries; thus children will always play on the edge of anything. They build castles on the edge of the sea, and can only be restrained by public proclamation and private violence from walking on the edge of the grass. For when we have come to the end of a thing we have come to the beginning of it.

Consequently, Belfort appears even more quintessentially French precisely because it lies on the very edge of Germany. Despite the German influences present in the area—such as German names, larger beer mugs, and theatrical barmaids dressed in exaggerated Alsatian costumes—the dominant French character seems to be intensified by these foreign elements. All day and night, groups of weary, sun-kissed soldiers trudge through the streets, emanating an air of stubborn disdain. German soldiers may exude contempt, but French soldiers possess a dual disdain, directed both at themselves and at others. This realism, perhaps, is an integral part of a nation skilled in war, science, and other undertakings that necessitate a blend of the essential and the unpleasant. And the soldiers and the civilians alike had most of them cropped hair, and that curious kind of head which to an Englishman looks almost brutal, the kind that we call a bullet-head. Indeed, we are speaking very appropriately when we call it a bullet-head, for in intellectual history the heads of Frenchmen have been bullets—yes, and explosive bullets.

.....

But there was a second reason why in this place one should think particularly of the open-air politics and the open-air art of the French. For this town of Belfort is famous for one of the most typical and powerful of the public monuments of France. From my café seat, I can gaze upon the hill that looms over the town, crowned by a substantial, flat-faced citadel, its many windows glowing in the evening sun. At the base of this steep hill rests a colossal stone lion, as imposing as the hill itself. It is hacked out of the rock with a sort of gigantic impression. No trivial attempt has been made to make it like a common statue; no attempt to carve the mane into curls, or to distinguish the monster minutely from the earth out of which he rises, shaking the world. The face of the lion has something of the bold conventionality of Assyrian art. The mane of the lion is left like a shapeless cloud of tempest, as if it might literally be said of him that God had clothed his neck with thunder. Even at this distance the thing looks vast, and in some sense prehistoric. Yet it was carved only a little while ago. It commemorates the town's unwavering resistance against the Germans throughout a harrowing year, surrendering only at the behest of its own government. Yet, the essence of defiance and resilience has pervaded this land since time immemorial.

As I depart this town and board a train into Germany, the news becomes increasingly urgent, filtering through the streets that Southern France is ablaze, hinting at the potential culmination of a grim modern struggle between wealth and poverty. And as I pass into quieter places for the last sign of France on the sky-line, I see the Lion of Belfort stand at bay, the last sight of that great people which has never been at peace.

The rain fell steadily as Victor Crummles stepped out onto the pavement. But he did not notice the fact. True, he put his umbrella up, but that was mere force of habit. He was not aware that he had put it up. His mind was far too engaged with the ordeal before him to permit any consciousness of external things to creep into it. He was "up against it and no mistake," he observed to himself. “I’m really in a bind,” he reminded himself, glancing at the piece of paper in his pocket that indicated where and when he was due for a medical examination. Reassuring himself, he confirmed its presence: Kilburn. Twelve o'clock.

Yes, he was fairly up against it. Not, as he hastened to assure himself, that he objected…. Not at all…. His patriotism ran deep, and he felt a strong desire to contribute to the war effort. He longed to take on the Germans and show them what he was made of. If only he had been younger, he thought; he would have enlisted without hesitation. That's what he'd have done—he'd have gone like a shot. No fetching him—if he'd been a bit younger. But at thirty-eight, he felt the weight of his age.

Here was the "Golden Crown." Yes, he thought he'd better have "just one." A drink would bolster his spirits and prepare him for the doctors. After all, he believed he ought to give them a fair chance, regardless of the potential ramifications for himself. A whisky-and-soda would just put him "in the pink."

There, that was better. Now he could face anything. Now for Kilburn. He contemplated his travel options. It was at least a two-mile journey—plenty of distance to cover. There was No. 16—he could take that. And there was the Tube—he could take that.

Or he could walk. There was time to spare. Yes, on the whole he thought he ought to walk. There was that varicose vein. The doctors ought to know about that. It wouldn't be fair to them or to the country that they shouldn't know about it. Varicose veins were serious conditions, and he had done his research. He could recall the definition clearly: It had made such a deep impression on him-that he could repeat what it said:—

“The dilation and thickening of veins, accompanied by lengthening and tortuosity, leading to the formation of knots or knobs, where blood coagulates, fibrin deposits, and sometimes even bone matter develops; additionally, the vein walls are diseased.”

There was more about it than that. It looked a very black case indeed. Many a man had been turned down for varicose veins, and—and—well, the doctors ought to know about it. That was all…. They ought to know about it…. He oughtn't to go there and pass himself off under false pretences…. Mind you, he wanted to fight the Germans all right. He wanted to do his bit—nobody more so. But was it fair not to let the doctors see what was the matter with him? He certainly had those knots and knobs when he walked very hard. Who knew? Perhaps there was "fibrin" and "osseous matter" there. At any rate, the doctors ought to see his leg under fair conditions….

He didn't hold with allowing your patriotism to make you deceive your country. He felt a moral duty to avoid deceiving his country, especially considering the financial resources that would be wasted on someone who might falter early in service. It wasn't fair to the fellow either. Not that he was thinking about himself…. Not at all. It was the country he was thinking of. A fellow must think about the country sometimes. It was his duty to put his own feelings, as it were, under the tap. He wanted to go to the war as much as any man, but he didn't want the country to lose by him….

Yes, he decided, it was his obligation to walk. It was crucial that he disclose the details of his varicose vein. He hoped it wouldn’t be a disqualifying factor, but he was committed to being forthright no matter the outcome. He was not the man to palm himself for what he wasn't. He would show the doctor quite plainly what his varicose vein was like.

When Victor finally entered the examination room, fatigue washed over him, but he steeled himself. He had taken another "stiffener" at the "Spread Eagle" and felt equal to any fate. The room was occupied by two doctors—one seated at a desk, the other standing near a window.

“Anything bothering you?” the seated doctor inquired.

"Not that I know," said Victor with the air of a man who meant business. However, he begrudgingly added, “I do have a bit of a varicose vein, but it’s hardly worth mentioning.”

“Oh, don’t worry about that,” the doctor assured him. “We’ve moved past that point. Now strip."

Don't worry about that! Moved past that point?” He had done his duty by mentioning the condition. If there was indeed fibrin or osseous matter in his veins, he had provided ample warning. It was the country that would suffer. Doctors could be so dismissive sometimes.

"Stripped? Now, let's have a look at you."

The doctor examined him carefully. Perhaps that varicose vein would surprise him after all. He had walked two miles, and it should be noticeable—though he didn’t necessarily wish for it to be. If his condition was significant, it was only fair that the doctors were informed.

“What did you say your age was?” the doctor asked.

"Thirty-eight, sir."

"Thirty-eight! Thirty-eight… um… Jeffkins!” the doctor called to his colleague, who joined him in assessing Victor.

They appeared to disregard his leg entirely. Well, it was their look out. He wouldn't be to blame if he broke down.

"You can dress." And the two doctors went to the window and consulted in low tones.

After a moment, the first doctor returned.

"Well, my man, it won't do," he said. “We admire your spirit… very commendable, indeed. But (laughing) thirty-eight! Come, come."

A realization struck Victor. Was he really being rejected?… And because he was too old?… Oh, the scandal, the shame…. And he dying to get at those Huns….

"But upon my oath…." He was really in earnest now.

"There, there, we understand," said the doctor. “You’ve done your best, and it’s commendable. And it's very creditable to you—very. But thirty-eight! Come, come…. Now, good morning."

Outside, Victor's anguish and indignation were too bitter to be borne unaided. He turned into the "Spread Eagle."

When I moved into a new house a few weeks ago, my books, as was natural, moved with me. Strong men, sweaty from exertion, packed them into boxes and lugged them to the moving van, grumbling about Caxton as they worked. On arrival at this end, they staggered with them into the room selected for my library, heaved off the lids of the cases, and awaited orders. The immediate need was for an emptier room. Together we hurried the books into the new white shelves which awaited them, the order in which they stood being of no matter so long as they were off the floor. Armful after armful was hastily stacked, the only pause being when (in the curious way in which these things happen) my own name suddenly caught the eye of the foreman. "Did you write this one, sir?" he inquired. I admitted it. "H'm," he said noncommittally. He glanced along the names of every armful after that, and appeared a little surprised at the number of books which I hadn't written. An easy-going profession, evidently.

Eventually, the books found their place on the shelves, and there they remain. I told myself that I would organize them properly when a rainy day presented itself. When that rainy day finally arrived, I instead pushed the task to some future morning. As they are now, I have to look along every shelf in the search for the book which I want. To come to Keats is no guarantee that we are on the road to Shelley. If he hasn’t mysteriously vanished, he’s likely wedged between How to Be a Golfer Though Middle-aged and something else equally perplexing.

Having written as far as this, I had to get up and see where Shelley really was. It is worse than I thought. He is currently lodged between Geometrical Optics and Studies in New Zealand Scenery. Ella Wheeler Wilcox, whom I find myself to be entertaining unawares, sits beside Anarchy or Order, which was apparently "sent in the hope that you will become a member of the Duty and Discipline Movement"—a vain hope, it would seem, for I have not yet paid my subscription. What I Found Out, by an English Governess, shares a corner with The Recreations of a Country Parson; they are followed by Villette and Baedeker's Switzerland. Something will have to be done about it. Yet, I find myself pondering what that action should be. If I gave you the impression that my books were precisely arranged in their old shelves, I misled you. They were arranged in the order known as "all anyhow." Perhaps they were slightly less "anyhow" than they are now, as volumes of the same work were at least grouped together, but that’s about the extent of their order. For years, I avoided the task of tidying them up, just as I’m continuing to do now. It is not laziness; it is simply that I don't know how to begin.

Let’s consider the idea of grouping all the poetry together. It sounds reasonable. But then Byron is eleven inches high (my tallest poet), and Beattie (my shortest) is just over four inches. How foolish they will look standing side by side. Perhaps you don't know Beattie, but I assure you that he was a poet. He wrote those majestic lines:—

"The shepherd-swain of whom I mention made On Scotia's mountains fed his little flock; The sickle, scythe or plough he never swayed— An honest heart was almost all his stock."

It’s hardly reasonable to expect a shepherd to wield a plow in the conventional manner, but Beattie appropriately highlighted that Edwin, the shepherd-swain, didn’t either. Edwin was the name of the shepherd- swain. "And yet poor Edwin was no vulgar boy," we are told a little further on in a line that should live. Well, having satisfied you that Beattie was really a poet, I can now return to my argument that an eleven-inch Byron cannot stand next to a four-inch Beattie, and be followed by an eight-inch Cowper, without making the shelf look silly. Yet, how could I possibly discard Beattie—Beattie, who wrote:

"And now the downy cheek and deepened voice Gave dignity to Edwin's blooming prime."

This reveals the conundrum. If one arranges books by their contents, the shelf quickly becomes untidy. Conversely, organizing them by size or color might produce an aesthetically pleasing display, but it risks obscuring Beattie from the poetically inclined visitor. Before, then, we decide what to do about it, we must ask ourselves that very awkward question, "Why do we have books on our shelves at all?" It is a most embarrassing question to answer.

Of course, you think that the proper answer (in your own case) is an indignant protest that you bought them in order to read them, and that yon put them on your shelves in order that you could refer to them when necessary. However, upon deeper reflection, one realizes how foolish that answer is. If reading were your sole purpose, why would some books be bound in luxurious morocco or half-calf covers? Why opt for a first edition when a hundredth edition could be acquired for much less? Why have you got half a dozen copies of The Rubaiyat? What is the particular value of this other book that you treasure it so carefully? Why, the fact that its pages are uncut. If you were to slice the pages open and read it, would that not diminish its value?

Thus, it becomes clear that your library serves a purpose beyond mere reference. You know as well as I do that it furnishes your room; that it furnishes it more effectively than does paint or mahogany or china. While it is certainly pleasant to have the books accessible for when you need them, such as when you’re writing an article on sea-bathing and need to recall Coleridge’s well-known words, the library is not only functional but also decorative. But do not let us be ashamed that we find it ornamental. Indeed, the more I survey it, the more I feel that my library is sufficiently ornamental as it stands. Any reassembling of the books might spoil the colour-scheme. For example, Baedeker's Switzerland and Villette are both red, a hue that is beautifully mirrored by a volume of Browning and Jevons' Elementary Logic after a brief interlude of blue. We had a woman here only yesterday who said, "How pretty your books look," and I am inclined to think that that is good enough. There is a careless rapture about them which I should lose if I started to arrange them methodically.

But perhaps I might risk this to the extent of getting all their heads the same way up. Yes, on one of these fine days (or wet nights) I shall take my library seriously in hand. There are still one or two books which are the wrong way round. I shall put them the right way round.

Reading the terms of the agreement which Charlie Chaplin refused in New York early in 1916 I had a kind of nervous collapse. For we English are not so accustomed to great sums of money as the Americans are. I wrapped a damp cloth around my head and attempted to analyze the staggering figures with a detached perspective, though it was challenging to do so when they resembled fortunes fit for kings. Chaplin was presented with a staggering ten thousand dollars a week for a year, amounting to £104,000 at the time, and significantly more today (in 1920). Additionally, he was offered a signing bonus of one hundred thousand dollars and fifty percent of any profits generated from his films after the payment of his salary. But it did not satisfy him. He refused it.

Now here is a most remarkable state of affairs—that the popular demand for laughter is such that a little acrobatic man with splay feet and a funny way with a cigarette, a hat, and a cane could be offered and could repudiate such colossal wealth as that, and for no other services than to clown it for the cinematoscope. The peculiarity of this scenario is heightened when one considers that these astounding figures emerged during wartime. Chaplin's ascent to wealth and influence coincided with one of history's most brutal conflicts.

If it is needful for so many people to hold their sides, Charlie's career is justified. He is also the first droll to conquer the whole world. I suppose that it is no exaggeration to say that at any moment of the day and night—allowing for divergences of time—it would be safe to maintain that ten million people are laughing at the Chaplin antics somewhere or other on this planet of ours. Wherever there is a community of more than two thousand people, it is reasonable to assume there exists a cinema; where there is a cinema, Chaplin's presence is often felt, even if not always in the latest release, as managers tend to be resourceful, showcasing older films as well. Does the Funniest Man on Earth, as he is called, I should like to know, realise what a rôle he fills? Does he stand before the glass and search the recesses of his countenance—which is now far more familiar to the world than any other—and marvel?

Charlie, by the way, has his private uses too. During a recent visit from a young friend, I found that the ordinary gulf that is fixed between a boy in the neighbourhood of ten and a man in the neighbourhood of five times that number was for once easily bridgeable. We found common ground, and very wisely stuck to it, in the circumstance that each of us had seen Charlie, and, by great good fortune, we had each seen him in his latest sketch. Whenever, therefore, a longueur threatened, I had but to mention another aspect of Charlie's genius, and in the discussion that followed all was well.

That Charlie is funny is beyond question. I will swear to that. His humor is so universal that it could resonate with a Tierra del Fuegan or a Bushman from Central Australia just as well as with ourselves, who might consider ourselves more cultured. One needs no civilised culture to appreciate the fun of the harlequinade, and to that has Charlie, with true instinct, returned. The essence of his comedy draws upon the traditional harlequinade, intensified and adapted for the discerning tastes of a growing audience in the film industry. It is also farce at its busiest, most furious. Charlie brought back that admirable form of humour which does not disdain the co-operation of fisticuffs, and in which, by way of variety, one man is aimed at, and another, too intrusive, is hit. However long the world may last, it is safe to say that the spectacle of one man receiving a blow meant for another will be popular.

What quickly becomes apparent is the extraordinary effort Chaplin invests compared to many of his more celebrated contemporaries in film. He is seldom absent from the screen, constantly in motion, and delivering a full performance. There is no physical humiliation he does not endure and inflict upon others. Such impartiality is rare in drama, where usually men are either on top or underneath. In the ordinary way our pet comedians must be on top and untouched. Even the clown, though he receives punishment en route , eventually triumphs. He seldom emerges victorious; instead, he embodies the quintessential victim of fate, always resilient in the face of adversity. His very essence is resiliency under difficulties, an unabashed and undefeatable front. His especial fascination to me is that life finds him always ready for it—not because he is armed by sagacity, but because he is even better armed by folly. He is first cousin to the village idiot, a natural child of nonsense, licensed up to the hilt, and (like Antæus) every time he rises from a knockdown blow he is the stronger.

It is a proof of the charter which the world has handed to this irresistible humourist that he has been permitted to introduce such an innovation in stage manners as the hitting of women. We only laugh the more when, having had his ears boxed by the fair, he retaliates with double strength. In one scene, he humorously extracts a lady in evening attire from a fountain, only to push her back in with glee. It takes someone of Chaplin's immense charm and innocence to make such a scenario seem acceptable, and his unpretentious nature allows audiences to embrace even the most absurd antics.

One significant reason for the widespread appeal of Chaplin's films—beyond the allure of the central character—is that they depict scenarios that could not occur in reality without legal consequences, and which often remain absent from traditional theater. I mean that men so freely assault each other; physical violence has the fullest and most abundant play. Every one longs to see kicks and blows administered, but is usually defrauded, and Charlie is a spendthrift with both. Charlie, however, is generous with his slapstick, delivering humor through kicks and punches with such cheerful spontaneity that one might wonder why such behavior hasn’t sparked a global trend. I know this—that a fat policeman with his back towards the exit of a cinema at the time a Chaplin film had ended would be in great danger from my foot were I then leaving. While I hope to maintain self-discipline, I cannot guarantee it; Chaplin's influence might just sanctify such an impulse. Film life and real life would merge into each other so naturally that if the policeman repaid me—or attempted to—in any other way but kind, I should feel outraged. To be arrested for it would be like a stab in the back from a friend.

How long Charlie will remain the darling of two hemispheres we must wait to see. But of one thing I am certain, and that is that if at any time the "The Funniest Man on Earth" ceases to compel laughter, he might by slightly changing his methods draw tears. He has the ability to entertain the most relentless seekers of joy, but he is equally equipped with the tools to evoke sadness. One of his melancholy smiles is really beautiful.

Once when I was very young I met one of those men who have made the Empire what it is—a man in an astracan coat, with an astracan moustache—a tight, black, curly moustache. Whether he put on the moustache with the coat or whether his Napoleonic will enabled him not only to grow a moustache in the usual place, but also to grow little moustaches all over his clothes, I do not know. I distinctly remember him telling me, “A man can’t get on nowadays by hanging about with his hands in his pockets.” To this, I flippantly retorted that perhaps success came from having one’s hands in others’ pockets. This prompted him to delve into a discussion on Moral Evolution, suggesting that my quip held some grain of truth. But the incident now comes back to me, and connects itself with another incident—if you can call it an incident—which happened to me only the other day.

I have only once in my life picked a pocket, and then (perhaps through some absent-mindedness) I picked my own. My act can really with some reason be so described. For in taking things out of my own pocket I had at least one of the more tense and quivering emotions of the thief; I had a complete ignorance and a profound curiosity as to what I should find there. Perhaps it would be the exaggeration of eulogy to call me a tidy person. But I can always pretty satisfactorily account for all my possessions. I always know their whereabouts and what I’ve done with them—unless they find their way into my pockets. If once anything slips into those unknown abysses, I wave it a sad Virgilian farewell. I suppose that the things that I have dropped into my pockets are still there; the same presumption applies to the things that I have dropped into the sea. But I regard the riches stored in both these bottomless chasms with the same reverent ignorance. It is said that the sea will reveal its hidden treasures on the last day, and I imagine that would also apply to the unusual items lurking in my pockets. But I have quite forgotten what any of them are; and there is really nothing (excepting the money) that I shall be at all surprised at finding among them.

.....

This encapsulates my previously untainted state of innocence. I here only wish briefly to recall the special, extraordinary, and hitherto unprecedented circumstances which led me in cold blood, and being of sound mind, to turn out my pockets. I found myself confined in a third-class train carriage for an extended journey. The time was towards evening, but it might have been anything, for everything resembling earth or sky or light or shade was painted out as if with a great wet brush by an unshifting sheet of quite colourless rain. I had no books or newspapers. I had not even a pencil and a scrap of paper with which to write a religious epic. There were no advertisements to peruse; otherwise, I could have delved into the depths of their printed words, as even the simplest phrase could ignite a cascade of mental exploration. Encountering a phrase like “Sunlight Soap” could lead me to ponder themes of sun worship, the mythology of Apollo, or the poetry of summer before reluctantly transitioning to the mundane topic of soap. But there was no printed word or picture anywhere; there was nothing but blank wood inside the carriage and blank wet without. Now I deny most energetically that anything is, or can be, uninteresting. So I stared at the joints of the walls and seats, and began thinking hard on the fascinating subject of wood. Just as I had begun to realise why, perhaps, it was that Christ was a carpenter, rather than a bricklayer, or a baker, or anything else, I suddenly started upright, and remembered my pockets. I was carrying about with me an unknown treasury. I had a British Museum and a South Kensington collection of unknown curios hung all over me in different places. I began to take the things out.

.....

The first thing I came upon consisted of piles and heaps of Battersea tram tickets. There were enough to equip a paper chase. They shook down in showers like confetti. These tickets evoked a wave of patriotic sentiment and even brought tears to my eyes. More importantly, they served as the printed material I craved, as I found brief yet compelling scientific essays about some kind of pill printed on their backs. In my state of destitution, those tickets could be considered a modest yet well-curated scientific library. If my train journey were to persist for a few more months, I could foresee myself deeply engaging in the debates surrounding the pill, crafting responses and counter-arguments based on the data at hand. However, it was the symbolic essence of those tickets that truly resonated with me. For as certainly as the cross of St. George means English patriotism, those scraps of paper meant all that municipal patriotism which is now, perhaps, the greatest hope of England.

The next thing that I took out was a pocket-knife. A pocketknife, as one can imagine, could warrant an entire volume filled with moral reflections. A knife typifies one of the most primary of those practical origins upon which as upon low, thick pillows all our human civilisation reposes. Metals, the mystery of the thing called iron and of the thing called steel, led me off half-dazed into a kind of dream. I saw into the intrails of dim, damp wood, where the first man among all the common stones found the strange stone. I imagined a fierce struggle where stone axes shattered and stone knives splintered against something gleaming and novel in the hands of a determined person. I could almost hear the clanging of hammers on anvils worldwide, and I visualized the swords of feudal conflicts and the scars of industrial warfare. For the knife is only a short sword; and the pocket-knife is a secret sword. I opened it and looked at that brilliant and terrible tongue which we call a blade; and I thought that perhaps it was the symbol of the oldest of the needs of man. Just as I formed this thought, I was surprised to find the next item emerging from my pocket was a box of matches. In that moment, I recognized fire—an element more potent than steel, an ancient and fierce force that we cherish yet approach with caution.

Continuing my exploration, I stumbled upon a piece of chalk, which evoked a vision of all the art and frescoes that have adorned our world. The next was a coin of a very modest value; and I saw in it not only the image and superscription of our own Caesar, but all government and order since the world began. But I have not space to say what were the items in the long and splendid procession of poetical symbols that came pouring out. I cannot tell you all the things that were in my pocket. I can tell you one thing, however, that I could not find in my pocket. I allude to my railway ticket.

Stevenson, as we recall, once dedicated his birthday to a young child—was it a girl or a boy? The child was fond of birthdays, while he had reached a time of life when they had ceased to have any interest for him. Many of us, if we live long enough, inevitably encounter this sense of indifference. The thrill of birthdays dissipates along with the toys that once sparked that joy. I remember when life was a journey from one birthday to another, the tedium of which was only relieved by such agreeable incidents as Christmas, Easter, and the school holidays. But for many years I have stumbled up against my birthday, as it were, with a shock of surprise, have given it a nod of recognition as one might greet an ancient acquaintance with whom one has lost sympathy, and have passed on without a further thought about the occasion.

Today, however, feels different. One cannot simply overlook the significance of turning fifty; it is a milestone that demands recognition. Fifty! Why, the Psalmist's limit is only seventy. Fifty from seventy. An easy sum, but what an impressive answer! Twenty years, and they the years of the sere, the yellow leaf. Only twenty more times to hear the cuckoo calling over the valley and see the dark beech woods bursting into tender green. I look back twenty years, and it seems only a span. And yet how remote fifty seemed in those days! It was so remote as to be hardly worth thinking about. To be fifty was to be among the old fellows, to be on the shelf, to have become an antiquity.

Now, standing at fifty years of age, I do not feel like an artifact at all; instead, I feel as youthful as I ever did. I had feared that entering middle age would bring with it a sense of nostalgia for the joys of my youth, a longing for the past that would make life feel unbearable. How would life be tolerable when cricket, for example, had ceased to play an important part in it? Never again to have the ecstasy of a drive along "the carpet" to the boundary or, with a flash of the arm, snapping an opponent in the slips. What a dreary desolation life must be, stripped of those joys! Yet, I’ve come to realize that the essence of youth is not contingent upon cricket or childhood delights. It is rooted in an acceptance of the possibilities life offers. Do not suppose, young fellow, that you are any younger than I am because you can jump five feet eight and I have ceased to want to jump at all. The spirit of youth is a far deeper and more persistent quality than mere physical prowess. It may be as vigorous at eighty as it is at eighteen. It is only its manner of expression which is changed. Holmes never admitted that he had grown old. "I am eighty-three young to-day," he would say. Likewise, Johnson, despite his age and ailments, insisted he was “a young fellow”—and indeed, he embodied a sprightly spirit that defied the ravages of time.

Youth is, in truth, not merely a physical condition but rather a matter of the soul. One can feel spiritually aged at twenty-five or retain a lively, youthful spirit at eighty. Byron was only thirty-four when he wrote:—

I am ashes where once I was fire. And the soul in my bosom is dead; What I loved I now merely admire, And my heart is as grey as my head.

Perhaps there was some affectation in this, for Byron was always dramatising himself. But that he died an old man at thirty-six is as indisputable as that Browning died a young man at seventy-seven, with that triumphant envoi of Asolando as his last expression of the eternal youth of the soul.

In thinking of old age, the mistake is to assume that the spirit must decay with the body. Naturally, if the body is treated poorly, its consequences will affect the spirit. But the natural decline of the physical powers leaves the healthy spirit untouched with age, should indeed leave it strengthened—glowing not with passion but with a steadier fire. When we are young in years our eager spirit cries for the moon.

We look before and after, And pine for what is not.

But as we get older we learn to be satisfied with something nearer than the moon. The scope of our aspirations may narrow, but the vastness of our existence remains unchanged, leading to the realization that what truly matters is often right at our fingertips. It is the homing of the spirit. We have been avid of the "topless grandeurs" of life, and we return to find that the spiritual satisfactions we sought were all the time within very easy reach. And in cultivating those satisfactions intensively we make another discovery. We find that this is the true way to the "topless grandeurs" themselves, for those topless grandeurs are not without us but within.

I fear I might be preaching now, and that is not my intention, yet if there were ever a time to reflect on such matters, it would be as I celebrate my fifty years. Let me as an antidote recall a little story which the present Bishop of Chester once told me over the dinner table, for it contains a practical recipe for keeping the heart young. In his younger days, he worked with Archdeacon Jones of Liverpool, who, at over eighty, had once been a tutor to Gladstone. The Archdeacon, then over eighty, had been tutor to Gladstone, and one day the future Bishop turned the conversation into a reminiscent channel, and sought to evoke the Archdeacon's memories of the long past. Suddenly, the Archdeacon shifted the topic, asking, “What was the Philharmonic concert like last night?” And then, in answer to the obvious surprise which the question had aroused, he added, "Although I am an old man, I want to keep my heart young, and the best way of doing that is not to let one's thoughts live in the past, but to keep them in tune with the life around one."

The truth is that every stage of the journey has its own interests. None is necessarily superior to another, though I have always favored the stage in which I currently find myself. At twenty, I believed there was no age quite like that, and now that I am fifty, I have transferred my enthusiasm to this present age. There is no age like it, I feel, for all-round enjoyment. I genuinely believe that if fortune permits me to reach sixty, I will proclaim that there is no age like sixty. And why not? It is pleasant to see the sun on the morning hills, but it is not less pleasant to walk home when the shadows are lengthening and the cool of the evening has come.
