Two soldiers, clearly siblings, were positioned at the entrance of a railway carriage—one seated within the compartment, the other standing on the platform.

"Now, you won't forget to write, Bill," said the latter.

"No," said Bill. "I shall be back at—tonight, and I'll write all round to-morrow. But, goodness, what a task! There's mother and the missus and Bob and Sarah and Aunt Jane and Uncle Jim, and—well, you know the lot. You’ve had to do it, Sam."

"Yes," said Sam, ruefully; "it's a fair teaser."

"And if you write to one and overlook another, they all get upset," Bill continued. "But I always mention all of 'em. I say 'love to Sarah,' and 'hope Aunt Jane's cold's better,' and that sort of thing, and that fills out a page. But I'm blowed if I can find anything else to say. I just begin 'hoping this finds you well, as it leaves me at present,' and then I'm done. What else can I say?"

"Nothing," said Sam, mournfully. "I just sit and scratch my head over the blessed paper, but nothing'll come. Seems as though my head's as empty as a drum."

"Same here. 'Tisn't like writing love-letters. When I was up to that game 'twas easy enough. When I got stuck I just put in half a page of crosses, and that filled up fine. But writing to mother and the missus and Sarah and Jim and the rest is different. You can’t just fill it with doodles; that would look ridiculous."

"Quite right," Sam agreed.

As the train began to pull away, the soldier inside settled back into his seat, pulled out a cigarette, and lit it. I found he had been twice out at the front, and was now home on sick leave. He had participated in the battle of Mons, experienced the retreat to the Marne, advanced to the Aisne, fought in the first battle of Ypres, and engaged in the fighting at Festubert. In a word, he had seen some of the greatest events in the world's history, face to face, and yet he confessed that when he came to writing a letter, even to his wife, he could find nothing to say. He was much like a woman mentioned by Horace Walpole, whose correspondence began and ended with the statement: "I write to you because I have nothing to do: I finish because I have nothing to say."

I suppose there has never been so much letter-writing in the world as is going on to-day, and much of it is good writing, as the papers show. But the case of my companion in the train is the case of thousands and tens of thousands of young fellows who for the first time in their lives want to write and discover that they have no gift of self-expression. It is not that they are stupid. It is that somehow the act of writing paralyses them. They cannot condense the atmosphere in which they live to the concrete word. You have to draw them out. They require encouragement to articulate their feelings. Once prompted, they can articulate their thoughts perfectly well, but without that nudge, they remain silent.

In the great sense letter-writing is no doubt a lost art. The introduction of the penny post and the fast pace of modern life have contributed to its decline. When Madame de Sévigny, Cowper, Horace Walpole, Byron, Lamb, and the Carlyles wrote their immortal letters the world was a leisurely place where there was time to indulge in the luxury of writing to your friends. And the cost of franking a letter made that letter a serious affair. If you could only send a letter once in a month or six months, and then at heavy expense, it became a matter of first-rate consequence. The less fortunate, of course, could hardly partake in the luxury of letter-writing. De Quincey tells us how the dalesmen of Lakeland a century ago used to dodge the postal charges. A letter arriving by stagecoach would be received by a mother who, upon glancing at the address and recognizing a certain mark indicating her son was well, would return it unopened to the carrier. In those days a letter was an event.

Today, however, with the ability to send a letter across the globe for a mere penny and postal services delivering multiple times a day, many of us do not take letter-writing seriously. Carlyle saw that the advent of the penny post would kill the letter by making it cheap. "I shall send a penny letter next time," he wrote to his mother when the cheap postage was about to come in, and he foretold that people would not bother to write good letters when they could send them for next to nothing. He was correct; the telegraph, the telephone, and the postcard have further contributed to the decline of this once revered form of communication. The rarity or difficulty of obtaining something often elevates its value. If diamonds were as plentiful as pebbles we shouldn't stoop to pick them up.

Yet, the situation for Bill, Sam, and countless others today diverges from this trend. They don't want to write literary letters, but they do want to tell the folks at home something about their life and the great things of which they are a part. But the great things are too great for them. They cannot put them into words. And they ought not to try, for the secret of letter-writing is intimate triviality. Bill might not be able to narrate the retreat from Mons, but he could share, as he did with me, the story of the blister on his heel, his yearning for a cigarette, the endless marches that left him exhausted, losing his friend at Le Cateau, or how his boot sole fell off at Meaux. And through such trivialities he would have given a living picture of the great retreat.

In short, to write a good letter you must approach the job in the lightest and most casual way. You must be personal, not abstract. One should not dismiss the significance of everyday occurrences as too trivial to mention. You must say, "This is just the sort of small thing we talk about at home. If I tell them this they will see me, as it were, they'll hear my voice, they'll know what I'm about." That is the purpose of a letter. Keats encapsulated this concept beautifully in one of his extensive letters addressed to his brother George and his wife in America, where he expressed the depth of familial affection that characterized his nature. He has described how he had been to see his mother, how she had laughed at his bad jokes, how they went out to tea at Mrs. Millar's, and how in going they were struck with the light and shade through the gateway at the Horse Guards. And he goes on: "I intend to write you such volumes that it will be impossible for me to keep any order or method in what I write; that will come first which is uppermost in my mind, not that which is uppermost in my heart—besides I should wish to give you a picture of our lives here whenever by a touch I can do it; even as you must see by the last sentence our walk past Whitehall all in good health and spirits—this I am certain of because I felt so much pleasure from the simple idea of your playing a game of cricket."

There is the recipe by one of the masters of the craft. A letter written in this vein annihilates distance; it continues the personal gossip, the intimate communion, that has been interrupted by separation; it preserves one's presence in absence. It should never be too simple, too ordinary, or too conversational. Its familiarity is not its weakness, but its supreme virtue. Should it strive for order, grandeur, or elaboration, it may turn into a fine essay yet will undoubtedly fail as a letter.

The Bar has always struck me as the most esteemed of professions, a field where its practitioners can maintain their dignity, no matter the circumstances. This is not the case with other professions. A schoolmaster can be referred to contemptuously as an usher; a doctor is regarded humorously as a licensed murderer; a solicitor is always retiring to gaol for making away with trust funds, and, in any case, is merely an attorney; while a civil servant sleeps from ten to four every day, and is only waked up at sixty in order to be given a pension. But there is no humorous comment to be made upon the barrister—unless it is to call him "my learned friend." Their claim to professionalism carries more weight than that of an actor. I don't know why. Perhaps it is because he walks about the Temple in a top-hat.

Many of my acquaintances have dabbled in the legal profession, having “eaten dinners” at the Inns of Court, making it challenging to voice any criticism of their chosen path. Additionally, one can never be too certain when one might find themselves in need of legal representation. However, I shall take the risk, and put the barrister in the dock. "Ladies and gentlemen of the jury, consider this well-tailored individual before you. What shall we say about him?"

Let us begin by asking ourselves what we expect from a profession. First and foremost, we undoubtedly seek a livelihood, yet I believe we desire something beyond mere financial compensation. If we were offered a thousand a year to walk from Charing Cross to Barnet every day, reasons of poverty might compel us to accept the offer, but we should hardly be proud of our new profession. We should prefer to earn a thousand a year by doing some more useful work. Indeed, to a man of any fine feeling the profession of Barnet walking would only be tolerable if he could persuade himself that by his exertions he was helping to revive the neglected art of pedestrianism, or to make more popular the neglected beauties of Barnet; if he could hope that, after his three- hundredth journey, inquisitive people would begin to follow him, wondering what he was after, and so come suddenly upon the old Norman church at the cross-roads, or, if they missed this, at any rate upon a much better appetite for their dinner. That is to say, he would have to persuade himself that he was walking, not only for himself, but also for the community.

It seems to me, then, that a profession is a noble or an ignoble one, according as it offers or denies to him who practises it the opportunity of working for some other end than his own advancement. A doctor collects fees from his patients, but he is aiming at something more than pounds, shillings, and pence; he is out to put an end to suffering. A schoolmaster earns a living by teaching, but he does not feel that he is fighting only for himself; he is a crusader on behalf of education. Artists, regardless of their chosen medium, seek to convey a message to the world, sharing their truths—which may benefit them but are not solely for their profit. All these and a thousand other ways of living have something of nobility in them. We enter them full of high resolves. We tell ourselves that we will follow the light as it has been revealed to us; that our ideals shall never be lowered; that we will refuse to sacrifice our principles to our interests. Yet, we inevitably stumble. The painter, lured by financial success, churns out repetitive works. The doctor neglects research and cultivates instead a bedside manner. The schoolmaster drops all his theories of education and conforms hastily to those of his employers. We fail, but it is not because the profession is an ignoble one; we had our chances. Indeed, the light is still there for those who look. It beckons to us.

Now, what about the Bar? Does a barrister strive for anything beyond personal advancement? He follows what gleam? What are his ideals? It matters little whether they succeed more or less frequently than others in reaching these ideals; what I seek to understand is what motivates them. I only want to know what it is that he is after. In the quiet hours when we are alone with ourselves and there is nobody to tell us what fine fellows we are, we come sometimes upon a weak moment in which we wonder, not how much money we are earning, nor how famous we are becoming, but what good we are doing. If a barrister experiences such an introspective moment, what reassurance can they draw from it? The only solace may lie in the belief that they are contributing to the administration of Justice. If he is to be proud of his profession, and in that lonely moment tolerant of himself, he must feel that he is taking a noble part in the vindication of legal right, the punishment of legal wrong. But he must do more than this. Just as the doctor, with increased knowledge and experience, becomes a better fighter against disease, advancing himself, no doubt, but advancing also medical science; just as the schoolmaster, having learnt new and better ways of teaching, can now give a better education to his boys, increasing thereby the sum of knowledge; so the barrister must be able to tell himself that the more expert he becomes as an advocate, the better will he be able to help in the administration of this Justice which is his ideal.

Can he tell himself this? I do not see how he can. His increased expertness will be of increased service to himself, of increased service to his clients, but no ideal will be the better served by reason of it. Consider a hypothetical case, Smith v. Jones. Counsel is briefed for Smith. After examining the case he tells himself in effect this: "As far as I can see, the Law is all on the other side. Luckily, however, sentiment is on our side. Given an impressionable jury, there's just a chance that we might pull it off. It's worth trying." He proceeds, and if he is sufficiently skilled, he secures a victory. A triumph for himself, but what has happened to the ideal? Did he ever contemplate, “I must do my utmost for my client, even if he is in the wrong, and hope for a loss?” I imagine not. The whole teaching of the Bar is that he must not bother about justice, but only about his own victory. Ultimately, what is the true pursuit of a barrister? What does the Bar provide beyond the allure of financial rewards?

I asked just now what were a barrister's ideals. Let’s reframe the question: What does it mean to be an ideal barrister? If we were to casually define an ideal doctor, we wouldn’t necessarily envision a prestigious figure on Harley Street. An ideal teacher does not equate to the Headmaster of Eton or the proprietor of a lucrative preparatory school. But can there be an ideal barrister other than a successful barrister? The eager young writer, just beginning a literary career, might fix his eyes upon Francis Thompson rather than upon Sir Hall Caine; the eager young clergyman might dream dreams over the Life of Father Damien more often than over the Life of the Archbishop of Canterbury; but to what star can the eager young barrister hitch his wagon, save to the star of material success? If he does not see himself as Sir Edward Carson, it is only because he thinks that perhaps after all Sir John Simon's manner is the more effective.

There may be other answers to the questions I have asked than the answers I have given, but it is no answer to ask me how the law can be administered without barristers. I cannot fathom how such a system could function without them, just as I find it hard to imagine how roads could be kept clean without someone to do the work. But that would not disqualify me from saying that road- sweeping was an unattractive profession. So also I am entitled to my opinion about the Bar, which is this. That because it offers material victories only and never spiritual ones, that because there can be no standard by which its disciples are judged save the earthly standard, that because there is no place within its ranks for the altruist or the idealist—for these reasons the Bar is not one of the noble professions.

Whatever is it that we are all looking for? I fancy that it is really quite close. When I was a boy I had a fancy that Heaven or Fairyland or whatever I called it, was immediately behind my own back, and that this was why I could never manage to see it, however often I twisted and turned to take it by surprise. I had a notion of a man perpetually spinning round on one foot like a teetotum in the effort to find that world behind his back which continually fled from him. Perhaps this is the reason the world spins. It is as if the world is forever attempting to glance over its shoulder in pursuit of the elusive realm that it cannot exist without.

In any case, as I have said, I think that we must always conceive of that which is the goal of all our endeavours as something which is in some strange way near. While science takes pride in discussing the vast distances of its celestial bodies and the daunting remoteness of the phenomena it examines, poetry and religion insist on the immediacy of their subjects, often highlighting their unnerving nearness. The Kingdom of Heaven is always described as being "At Hand," while Looking-glass Land is merely a reflection through the glass. So I for one should never be astonished if the next twist of a street led me to the heart of that maze in which all the mystics are lost. I should not be at all surprised if I turned one corner in Fleet Street and saw a yet queerer-looking lamp; I should not be surprised if I turned a third corner and found myself in Elfland.

However, what did catch me off guard recently was something far more unexpected. I ventured out of Fleet Street and unexpectedly found myself in England.

The peculiar shock I felt likely merits some explanation. In the darkest or the most inadequate moments of England there is one thing that should always be remembered about the very nature of our country. It may be shortly stated by saying that England is not such a fool as it looks. The types of England, the externals of England, always misrepresent the country. England operates as an oligarchy, deliberately presenting an elite that seems inferior to the general populace.

The speaking in the House of Commons, for instance, is not only worse than the speaking was, it is worse than the speaking is, in all or almost all other places in small debating clubs or casual dinners. Our countrymen probably prefer this solemn futility in the higher places of the national life. It may be a strange sight to see the blind leading the blind; but England provides a stranger. England shows us the blind leading the people who can see. And this again is an under-statement of the case. For the English political aristocrats not only speak worse than many other people; they speak worse than themselves. The ignorance of statesmen is like the ignorance of judges, an artificial and affected thing. If you have the good fortune really to talk with a statesman, you will be constantly startled with his saying quite intelligent things. It makes one nervous at first. And I have never been sufficiently intimate with such a man to ask him why it was a rule of his life in Parliament to appear sillier than he was.

It is the same with the voters. The average man votes below himself; he votes with half a mind or with a hundredth part of one. A man ought to vote with the whole of himself as he worships or gets married. When casting a vote, one ought to engage their intellect and emotions, their spirit and physical instincts, their appreciation for beauty and their love for music. If he has ever seen a fine sunset, the crimson colour of it should creep into his vote. If they have been moved by beautiful melodies, those songs should echo in their ears as they make that sacred mark. Yet, the challenge confronting English democracy at every election is that it often represents something less than its true potential. The issue is not merely that a minority of the electorate participates; rather, it is that a minority of those who vote truly engage with the process.

This is the tragedy of England; you cannot judge it by its foremost men. Its types do not typify. On the occasion I reference, I discovered this to be particularly true of a once-vibrant middle class, which I assumed had nearly disappeared from existence. It appeared to me that the primary representatives of this class had all drifted in different directions; they had either pursued the allure of the Smart Set or sought the simplicity of the Simple Life. Personally, I find it difficult to favor one over the other; those individuals may keep either—or, more likely, both—alternatively succumbing to the sickness of each. But all the prominent men who plainly represent the middle class have adopted either the single eye-glass of Mr. Chamberlain or the single eye of Mr. Bernard Shaw.

This old class I speak of lacks a true representative. Its food was plentiful; but it had no show. Its food was plain; but it had no fads. It was serious about politics; and when it spoke in public it committed the solecism of trying to speak well. I thought that this old earnest political England had practically disappeared. And as I say, I took one turn out of Fleet Street and I found a room full of it.

.....

At the top of the room was a chair in which Johnson had sat. The club was a club in which Wilkes had spoken, in a time when even the ne’er-do-weel was virile. However, one could argue that these historical references might merely denote a bygone era. The extraordinary thing was that this hall had all the hubbub, the sincerity, the anger, the oratory of the eighteenth century. The members of this club were of all shades of opinion, yet there was not one speech which gave me that jar of unreality which I often have in listening to the ablest men uttering my own opinion. The Toryism of this club was like the Toryism of Johnson, a Toryism that could use humour and appealed to humanity. The democracy of this club was like the democracy of Wilkes, a democracy that can speak epigrams and fight duels; a democracy that can face things out and endure slander; the democracy of Wilkes, or, rather, the democracy of Fox.

One thing especially filled my soul with the soul of my fathers. Each man speaking, whether he spoke well or ill, spoke as well as he could from sheer fury against the other man. This marks a significant decline in our modern political discourse. Today, a speaker does not become more oratorical as their sincerity deepens. An eighteenth-century speaker, when he got really and honestly furious, looked for big words with which to crush his adversary. The new speaker looks for small words to crush him with. He looks for little facts and little sneers. In a modern speech the rhetoric is put into the merely formal part, the opening to which nobody listens. When a politician—be it Mr. Chamberlain, a moderate figure, or a more radical socialist—becomes truly sincere, their discourse degenerates into something coarse, punctuated by phrases like, “Where do we come in?” or “It’s your money they want.”

The men in this eighteenth-century club were entirely different; they were quite eighteenth century. Each one rose to his feet quivering with passion, and tried to destroy his opponent, not with sniggering, but actually with eloquence. I found myself debating with them on the topic of Home Rule, and ultimately expressed my belief that the English aristocracy held disdain for the idea of an Irish Parliament because it would resemble their own club.

As I exited the club and stepped back into Fleet Street under the dim glow of a streetlamp, I stumbled upon a crude poster about Wastrels, claiming that London was rising against something hardly anyone had heard of.

Suddenly, it struck me, almost like a vivid tableau: the modern world resembles a vast and tempestuous ocean, teeming with monstrous, living entities. And I saw that across the top of it is spread a thin, a very thin, sheet of ice, of wicked wealth and of lying journalism.

Standing there in the shadows, I could almost hear that ice beginning to crack.

Some time ago I wrote in these columns an article called “The Extraordinary Cabman.” Today, I have the opportunity to recount an even more remarkable experience involving a cab. What made this cab so extraordinary was its distinct aversion to me; it ejected me forcefully right in the middle of the Strand. If my friends who read the DAILY NEWS are as romantic (and as rich) as I take them to be, I presume that this experience is not uncommon. It stands to reason that many of them may have also found themselves unceremoniously tossed from cabs across London. Still, as there are some people, virginal and remote from the world, who have not yet had this luxurious experience, I will give a short account of the psychology of myself when my hansom cab ran into the side of a motor omnibus, and I hope hurt it.

I do not need to dwell on the essential romance of the hansom cab—that one really noble modern thing which our age, when it is judged, will gravely put beside the Parthenon. It is really modern in that it is both secret and swift. My particular hansom cab exemplified these traits, though it met with unfortunate circumstances as well. But it is also English; it is not to be found abroad; it belongs to a beautiful, romantic country where nearly everybody is pretending to be richer than they are, and acting as if they were. It is comfortable, and yet it is reckless; and that combination is the very soul of England. But although I had always realised all these good qualities in a hansom cab, I had not experienced all the possibilities, or, as the moderns put it, all the aspects of that vehicle. My previous assertions regarding the merits of such vehicles were made while they were upright. Therefore, allow me to convey my feelings during that fateful moment when I was unceremoniously ejected from a hansom cab for what I hope is the first and last time. Polycrates threw one ring into the sea to propitiate the Fates. I have thrown one hansom cab into the sea (if you will excuse a rather violent metaphor) and the Fates are, I am quite sure, propitiated. Though I am told they do not like to be told so.

I was driving yesterday afternoon in a hansom cab down one of the sloping streets into the Strand, reading one of my own admirable articles with continual pleasure, and still more continual surprise, when the horse fell forward, scrambled a moment on the scraping stones, staggered to his feet again, and went forward. The horses in my cabs often do this, and I have learnt to enjoy my own articles at any angle of the vehicle. So I did not see anything at all odd about the way the horse went on again. However, a glance at the faces of the pedestrians revealed a stark change; they were transfixed with fear, as if struck by a bolt of lightning. And one man half ran out into the road with a movement of the elbow as if warding off a blow, and tried to stop the horse. Then I knew that the reins were lost, and the next moment the horse was like a living thunder-bolt. I try to describe things exactly as they seemed to me; many details I may have missed or mis-stated; many details may have, so to speak, gone mad in the race down the road. I remember that I once called one of my experiences narrated in this paper “A Fragment of Fact.” This is, at any rate, a fragment of fact. No fact could possibly be more fragmentary than the sort of fact that I expected to be at the bottom of that street.

I am a firm believer in addressing those who already hold certain convictions, for I have often found that they do not fully grasp the depth of their own beliefs.

Thus I have always urged in this paper that democracy has a deeper meaning than democrats understand; that is, that common and popular things, proverbs, and ordinary sayings always have something in them unrealised by most who repeat them. Here is one. We have all heard about the man who is in momentary danger, and who sees the whole of his life pass before him in a moment. In the stark, literal sense, this is an outright fabrication. No one can claim that during a crisis, they meticulously recalled every event, every ticket they ever purchased to Wimbledon, or the countless times they shared brown bread and butter.

But in those few moments, while my cab was tearing towards the traffic of the Strand, I discovered that there is a truth behind this phrase, as there is behind all popular phrases. I did really have, in that short and shrieking period, a rapid succession of a number of fundamental points of view. I went through what might be described as five distinct religions in the span of just a few seconds. My first religion was pure Paganism, which among sincere men is more shortly described as extreme fear. This state was soon succeeded by a mindset that, while real, defies proper nomenclature. The ancients might have referred to it as Stoicism, and perhaps it aligns with what some German philosophers mean when they discuss Pessimism. It was an empty acceptance of whatever fate had in store, as if I had transcended the significance of it all. And then, curiously enough, came a very strong contrary feeling—that things mattered very much indeed, and yet that they were something more than tragic. It was a feeling, not that life was unimportant, but that life was much too important ever to be anything but life. I hope this realization was a reflection of Christianity; at least, it coincided with the moment of our collision with the omnibus.

In what felt like a surreal twist, the hansom cab seemed to topple over me, enveloping me like a massive hood. I then found myself crawling out from underneath it in attitudes so undignified that they must have added enormously to that great cause to which the Anti-Puritan League and I have recently dedicated ourselves. I mean the cause of the pleasures of the people. As to my demeanour when I emerged, I have two confessions to make, and they are both made merely in the interests of mental science. First, just moments before the collision, I had been in a seemingly serene state of mind; however, upon standing up and realizing I had sustained only minor cuts, I began, much like St. Peter, to unleash a torrent of curses. A man offered me a newspaper or something that I had dropped. I can distinctly remember consigning the paper to a state of irremediable spiritual ruin. I am very sorry for this now, and I apologise both to the man and to the paper. I have not the least idea what was the meaning of this unnatural anger; I mention it as a psychological confession. It was immediately followed by extreme hilarity, and I made so many silly jokes to the policeman that he disgraced himself by continual laughter before all the little boys in the street, who had hitherto taken him seriously.

.....

There is one other odd thing about the matter which I also mention as a curiosity of the human brain or deficiency of brain. Every three minutes or so, I found myself reminding the policeman that I had yet to pay the cabman and fervently hoped he would not suffer a financial loss. The officer reassured me that everything would be fine and that the cabman would show up. But it was not until about half an hour afterwards that it suddenly struck me with a shock intolerable that the man might conceivably have lost more than half a crown; that he had been in danger as well as I. I had instinctively regarded the cabman as something uplifted above accidents, a god. I immediately made inquiries, and I am happy to say that they seemed to have been unnecessary.

But henceforward I shall always understand with a darker and more delicate charity those who take tythe of mint, and anise, and cumin, and neglect the weightier matters of the law; I shall remember how I was once really tortured with owing half a crown to a man who might have been dead. Some dedicated gentlemen in white coats at Charing Cross Hospital attended to my minor injuries, after which I stepped back out into the bustling Strand. A sense of unnatural youth enveloped me, igniting a yearning for uncharted experiences. So to open a new chapter in my life I got into a hansom cab.
